lede: SOH CAH TOA needs a right angle, and most triangles do not have one: two legs of a walk, a roof truss, a plot of land. Three formulae take over, the sine rule, the cosine rule and an area formula, and all three are printed on your paper.
can: Label a triangle so each small letter faces its capital.
Choose the sine rule or the cosine rule from what is marked.
Find an area, a side or an angle, and chain the rules.

alt: Triangle PQR. The side QR, opposite P, is labelled p equals 6 cm; PR is labelled q; PQ is labelled r equals 7 cm; the angle at P is 50 degrees.
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 340" role="img"><title>Triangle PQR with each side named after the angle it faces</title><path d="M65.3 276 L334.7 276 L243.2 64 Z" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="50.8" y="287.9" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">P</text><text x="348.5" y="289.1" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">Q</text><text x="246.4" y="53.3" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">R</text><text x="301.8" y="169.5" font-size="15" text-anchor="start" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">p = 6 cm</text><text x="143.5" y="166" font-size="15" text-anchor="end" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">q</text><text x="200" y="295" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">r = 7 cm</text><path d="M89.3 276 A24 24 0 0 0 80.7 257.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="105.2" y="262.4" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">50°</text></svg>
caption: Each side takes the small letter of the angle it faces: QR is p, PR is q, PQ is r.

md: Every triangle has three sides and three angles, and each side faces exactly one angle. That pairing is the whole language of this topic: the side facing angle $A$ is called $a$, the side facing $B$ is $b$, and the side facing $C$ is $c$. A side faces the angle it does not touch.

Label before anything else. The sine rule pairs a side with the angle facing it, so finding one complete pair, a known side and the known angle opposite it, tells you the sine rule can start. Without a complete pair, the cosine rule is the tool.

stem: In triangle $PQR$, $PQ = 7$ cm, $QR = 6$ cm and angle $P = 50°$. Name each side, and say whether there is a complete pair.

steps.decision: A side takes the small letter of the vertex it does not touch.
$PR$ misses $Q$, and $PQ$ misses $R$.
A known side with its known opposite angle is exactly what the sine rule needs to start.

prompt: In triangle $ABC$, which side is opposite angle $A$?
explain: As in step 1 of See it: the side opposite an angle is the one that does not touch it. $AB$ and $AC$ both meet at $A$; only $BC$ misses $A$, so $BC$ is $a$.

twin.prompt: In triangle $XYZ$, which side is opposite angle $Z$?
twin.explain: The side opposite $Z$ is the one that does not touch $Z$. $XZ$ and $YZ$ both end at $Z$, so it is $XY$, the side called $z$.

optionNotes.why: $XZ$ ends at $Z$, so it is next to the angle, not opposite it. It is $y$, the side facing $Y$.
$YZ$ ends at $Z$, so it is next to the angle. It is $x$, the side facing $X$.
$AB$ starts at $A$, so it is one of the two sides next to the angle. It faces $C$, so it is $c$.
$AC$ also starts at $A$. It faces $B$, so it is $b$, not $a$.

alt: Triangle ABC with a dashed perpendicular h from C down to AB. The side AC is labelled b and BC is labelled a; a right-angle mark sits where the height meets AB.
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 246" role="img"><title>A perpendicular height h splits triangle ABC into two right-angled triangles</title><path d="M46 200 L354 200 L161.5 46 Z" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="161.5" y1="46" x2="161.5" y2="200" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="30.6" y="209.4" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">A</text><text x="369.6" y="208.5" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">B</text><text x="158.9" y="35.2" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">C</text><text x="92.6" y="119.6" font-size="15" text-anchor="end" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">b</text><text x="266.5" y="117.1" font-size="15" text-anchor="start" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">a</text><text x="151.5" y="128" font-size="15" text-anchor="end" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">h</text><path d="M172.5 200 L172.5 189 L161.5 189" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/></svg>
caption: The height h from C splits ABC into two right-angled triangles, one with hypotenuse b and one with hypotenuse a.

md: The sine rule is not a new idea: it is right-angled trigonometry done twice. Drop a perpendicular of height $h$ from $C$ to $AB$. It cuts the triangle into two right-angled triangles, and $h$ belongs to both, so it can be written in two ways. Setting the two equal gives the rule.

stem: Show why $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}$ in triangle $ABC$.

steps.decision: In the left-hand right-angled triangle, $b$ is the hypotenuse and $h$ is opposite $A$.
In the right-hand triangle, $a$ is the hypotenuse and $h$ is opposite $B$.

steps.working: $b\sin A = a\sin B$, so $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}$
steps.decision: One height, two expressions. Dividing both sides by $\sin A \sin B$ gives the rule; dropping the height from another vertex brings in $c$ and $\sin C$.

prompt: In triangle $XYZ$, the perpendicular from $Z$ to $XY$ has length $h$. Which two expressions are both equal to $h$?
explain: As in See it: $y$ is $XZ$, the hypotenuse of the left-hand triangle, and $h$ is opposite $X$, so $h = y\sin X$. On the right, $x = YZ$ is the hypotenuse and $h$ is opposite $Y$, so $h = x\sin Y$.

twin.prompt: In triangle $PQR$, the perpendicular from $R$ to $PQ$ has length $h$. Which two expressions are both equal to $h$?
twin.explain: $q = PR$ is the hypotenuse of the triangle at $P$, with $h$ opposite $P$, so $h = q\sin P$. Likewise $p = QR$ with $h$ opposite $Q$ gives $h = p\sin Q$.

optionNotes.why: Each side has been paired with its own angle. The hypotenuse at $P$ is $PR$, which is $q$.
$r$ is $PQ$, the base the height falls on, not a hypotenuse. The hypotenuses are $q$ and $p$.
Each side has been paired with its own angle. In the left-hand triangle the hypotenuse is $XZ$, which is $y$, so $h = y\sin X$.
Cosine gives the side next to the angle. The height is opposite $X$ and opposite $Y$, so it is the sine that gives it.

text: 3. The sine rule for a side

alt: Triangle DEF with DE equal to 10 cm, the angle at D 43 degrees and the angle at E 74 degrees. The angle at F is not marked.
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 319" role="img"><title>Triangle DEF with two angles and one side</title><path d="M46 273 L354 273 L289 46.4 Z" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="31.2" y="284.1" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">D</text><text x="367.7" y="286.3" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">E</text><text x="294.9" y="36.5" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">F</text><text x="200" y="292" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">10 cm</text><path d="M70 273 A24 24 0 0 0 63.6 256.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="86.9" y="261.9" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">43°</text><path d="M347.4 249.9 A24 24 0 0 0 330 273" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="318.9" y="251.5" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">74°</text></svg>
caption: Two angles and a side: the third angle comes free, and then the sine rule finds any side.

md: With two angles and one side, the third angle comes free from $180°$, so every side now has a known opposite angle. Put the side you want on top: $\dfrac{DF}{\sin E} = \dfrac{DE}{\sin F}$, then multiply both sides by $\sin E$. Write the rule with its numbers before you calculate; that line is the method mark.

stem: In triangle $DEF$, angle $D = 43°$, angle $E = 74°$ and $DE = 10$ cm. Calculate $DF$, correct to 3 significant figures.

steps.decision: $DE$ faces $F$, so the known side's partner is found first.
$DF$ faces $E = 74°$. The side wanted goes on top.
Multiply both sides by sin 74°, key it in one go, round once.

title: Sine Rule missing sides
why: Corbettmaths labels and solves more sine-rule triangles at a steady pace. Watch the labelling come before every substitution.

prompt: $\dfrac{x}{\sin 40°} = \dfrac{8}{\sin 65°}$. Work out $x$, correct to 3 significant figures.
explain: As in step 3 of See it, multiply both sides by $\sin 40°$: $x = \dfrac{8 \sin 40°}{\sin 65°} = 5.6739\ldots$, so $5.67$ to 3 significant figures.

twin.prompt: $\dfrac{x}{\sin 35°} = \dfrac{12}{\sin 80°}$. Work out $x$, correct to 3 significant figures.
twin.explain: Multiply both sides by $\sin 35°$: $x = \dfrac{12 \sin 35°}{\sin 80°} = 6.9891\ldots$, so $6.99$ to 3 significant figures.

text: 4. The sine rule for an angle

alt: Triangle KLM with KM equal to 8 cm, LM equal to 11 cm and the angle at K 39 degrees. The angle at M is marked with an arc.
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 189" role="img"><title>Triangle KLM with two sides and a non-included angle</title><path d="M46 143 L354 143 L165.7 46.1 Z" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="30.4" y="151.5" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">K</text><text x="369.7" y="151.1" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">L</text><text x="160.4" y="36" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">M</text><text x="97" y="88.7" font-size="15" text-anchor="end" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">8 cm</text><text x="266.3" y="87.1" font-size="15" text-anchor="start" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">11 cm</text><path d="M70 143 A24 24 0 0 0 64.7 127.9" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="87.5" y="133.3" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">39°</text><path d="M147 61.2 A24 24 0 0 0 187 57.1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/></svg>
caption: LM = 11 cm faces the 39° angle: a complete pair. The sine rule gives the angle at L; 180° gives M.

md: For an angle, turn the rule upside down so the sine you want is on top: $\dfrac{\sin L}{KM} = \dfrac{\sin K}{LM}$. Multiply by $KM$, then take $\sin^{-1}$ once. If the question asks for a different angle, the angle sum finishes the job. The longer side faces the larger angle: a quick check that your answer is the right size.

stem: In triangle $KLM$, $KM = 8$ cm, $LM = 11$ cm and angle $K = 39°$. Calculate angle $KML$, correct to 1 decimal place.

steps.decision: $LM = 11$ faces $K$: a complete pair. $KM = 8$ faces $L$.
Multiply by 8, then $\sin^{-1}$ once. $L$ is smaller than $K$, as the shorter side faces it.
The angle asked for is at M, so the angle sum finishes it.

prompt: In triangle $ABC$, $BC = 12$ cm, $AC = 9$ cm and angle $A = 48°$. Calculate angle $ACB$, correct to 1 decimal place.
explain: As in See it: $BC$ faces $A$, a complete pair, and $AC$ faces $B$. So $\sin B = \dfrac{9 \sin 48°}{12}$, giving $B = 33.87\ldots°$, and angle $ACB = 180° - 48° - B = 98.1°$.

twin.prompt: In triangle $PQR$, $QR = 10$ cm, $PR = 7$ cm and angle $P = 52°$. Calculate angle $PRQ$, correct to 1 decimal place.
twin.explain: $QR$ faces $P$ and $PR$ faces $Q$, so $\sin Q = \dfrac{7 \sin 52°}{10}$ and $Q = 33.48\ldots°$. Then angle $PRQ = 180° - 52° - Q = 94.5°$.

text: 5. The cosine rule for a side

alt: Triangle ABC with AB equal to 7.5 cm, AC equal to 6 cm and the obtuse angle of 122 degrees between them at A. The side BC is unmarked.
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 239" role="img"><title>Two sides and the obtuse angle between them</title><path d="M137.7 193 L354 193 L46 46.3 Z" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="127.3" y="210.2" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">A</text><text x="369.4" y="202.3" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">B</text><text x="33.1" y="41.8" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">C</text><text x="245.8" y="212" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">7.5 cm</text><text x="80" y="132" font-size="15" text-anchor="end" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">6 cm</text><path d="M161.7 193 A24 24 0 0 0 125 172.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="159" y="159.5" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">122°</text></svg>
caption: Two sides and the angle between them: no complete pair, so the cosine rule finds the third side.

md: When the known angle sits between the two known sides, no side faces a known angle and the sine rule cannot start. The cosine rule, $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$, is Pythagoras with a correction for the angle. An obtuse angle has a negative cosine, so the correction is added and the side comes out longer.

title: Pythagoras is the 90° case
md: Put $A = 90°$ into the cosine rule: $\cos 90° = 0$, the correction disappears and $a^2 = b^2 + c^2$ is left. A sharper angle pulls the opposite side in, which is why the term is subtracted; an obtuse angle pushes it out.

stem: In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 7.5$ cm, $AC = 6$ cm and angle $A = 122°$. Calculate $BC$, correct to 3 significant figures.

steps.decision: $BC$ faces the $122°$: write the rule with every number in before calculating.
$\cos 122°$ is negative, so the term is added: the side is longer than Pythagoras would give.
The rule gives BC squared: take the square root, then round.

prompt: Two sides of a triangle are $9$ cm and $5$ cm, and the angle between them is $47°$. Calculate the third side, correct to 3 significant figures.
explain: As in See it: $a^2 = 9^2 + 5^2 - 2 \times 9 \times 5 \times \cos 47° = 44.62\ldots$. The square root gives $a = 6.6798\ldots$, so $6.68$ cm.

twin.prompt: Two sides of a triangle are $8$ cm and $12$ cm, and the angle between them is $105°$. Calculate the third side, correct to 3 significant figures.
twin.explain: $a^2 = 8^2 + 12^2 - 2 \times 8 \times 12 \times \cos 105° = 257.693\ldots$; the obtuse angle makes the term positive. So $a = 16.0528\ldots$, which is $16.1$ cm.

text: 6. The cosine rule for an angle

alt: A triangle with sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 11 cm. The angle at A, opposite the 11 cm side, is marked with an arc.
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 340" role="img"><title>Three sides and no angles</title><path d="M132.5 294 L323.1 294 L76.9 46 Z" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="124.8" y="313.1" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">A</text><text x="337" y="306.9" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">B</text><text x="68.6" y="37.3" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">C</text><text x="209.9" y="165.1" font-size="15" text-anchor="start" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">11 cm</text><text x="91" y="178.1" font-size="15" text-anchor="end" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">8 cm</text><text x="227.8" y="313" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">6 cm</text><path d="M156.5 294 A24 24 0 0 0 127.2 270.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/></svg>
caption: Three sides and no angle: the cosine rule, rearranged, finds any angle. The one facing 11 cm is the largest.

md: With three sides and no angle there is no pair at all, so the cosine rule is used backwards: $\cos A = \dfrac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$. This form is not printed on the formula sheet. The side facing the angle you want is the one subtracted. A negative cosine is not a mistake: it means the angle is obtuse.

stem: A triangle has sides $6$ cm, $8$ cm and $11$ cm. Calculate its largest angle, correct to 1 decimal place.

steps.working: The largest angle faces the $11$ cm side
steps.decision: Name the angle before you write anything: the longest side faces the largest angle.
The two sides that touch the angle are squared and added; the side facing it is subtracted.
The cosine is negative, so the angle is obtuse, as the longest side promised.

prompt: Three sides are 5, 7 and 9, and you want the angle facing the 9. Which square is subtracted on the top?
explain: As in step 2 of See it: the side facing the angle you want is subtracted, so $\cos A = \dfrac{5^2 + 7^2 - 9^2}{2 \times 5 \times 7}$. The two sides that touch the angle are the ones added.

twin.prompt: Three sides are 4, 6 and 8, and you want the angle facing the 6. Which square is subtracted on the top?
twin.explain: The side facing the angle is the one subtracted: $\cos A = \dfrac{4^2 + 8^2 - 6^2}{2 \times 4 \times 8}$. The 4 and the 8 touch the angle, so they are added.

optionNotes.why: The 8 is the longest side, but the angle wanted faces the 6. The side facing the angle is the one subtracted.
The 4 touches the angle, so it is one of the two squares added. The 6 faces it.
The 7 touches the angle you want, so it is added. Only the side facing the angle, 9, is subtracted.
The 5 is next to the angle, so it is one of the two squares added. The 9 faces it.

alt: A triangle with sides 13 cm and 9 cm meeting at a 35 degree angle.
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 214" role="img"><title>Two sides and the angle between them, for the area</title><path d="M46 168 L354 168 L220.7 45.7 Z" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="30.5" y="176.9" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">A</text><text x="369.4" y="177.3" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">B</text><text x="223.3" y="34.9" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600">C</text><text x="200" y="187" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">13 cm</text><text x="125.3" y="100.4" font-size="15" text-anchor="end" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">9 cm</text><path d="M70 168 A24 24 0 0 0 65.7 154.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="88" y="159.8" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor">35°</text></svg>
caption: Area = ½ab sin C uses the angle in the fork made by the two sides, here 35°.

md: Area $= \tfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ is half base times height in disguise: $a\sin C$ is the perpendicular height onto $b$. The angle must be the one between the two sides you use; any other angle gives a believable number and nothing warns you. The formula also runs backwards: given the area and two sides, $\sin C$ is the only unknown.

stem: Two sides of a triangle are $9$ cm and $13$ cm with an angle of $35°$ between them. Find the area; then find the angle if, instead, the area were $50$ cm$^2$.

steps.decision: The 35° is between the 9 and the 13, so it is the angle the formula wants.
One rounding, at the end.
Backwards: the area is given, so the formula is an equation with one unknown.
Take the inverse sine once.

prompt: Two sides of $7$ cm and $10$ cm meet at an angle of $40°$. Work out the area, correct to 3 significant figures.
explain: As in steps 1 and 2 of See it: the $40°$ is between the two sides, so area $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 7 \times 10 \times \sin 40° = 22.4976\ldots$, which is $22.5$ cm$^2$.

twin.prompt: Two sides of $6$ cm and $11$ cm meet at an angle of $72°$. Work out the area, correct to 3 significant figures.
twin.explain: Area $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 11 \times \sin 72° = 31.3849\ldots$, so $31.4$ cm$^2$. The $72°$ lies between the two sides, so it is the right angle to use.

prompt: A question gives the area of a triangle, two of its sides, and asks for the angle between them. What is your first line?
options: $\frac{1}{2} \times$ the two sides $\times \sin C =$ the given area
The cosine rule with the two sides
Nothing can be found until the third side is known
answer: $\frac{1}{2} \times$ the two sides $\times \sin C =$ the given area
explain: Steps 3 and 4 of See it: with the area known, the area formula has one unknown, $\sin C$, so it is an equation. Solve for $\sin C$, then take $\sin^{-1}$ once.

twin.prompt: A triangle has sides $8$ cm and $12$ cm and an area of $30$ cm$^2$. The angle between those sides is wanted. What is the first line?
twin.explain: The area is given, so put the area formula equal to it: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 12 \times \sin C = 30$, then $\sin C = \dfrac{30}{48}$. The cosine rule needs a third side, and 30 is an area.

optionNotes.why: The half has gone. Without it $\sin C$ comes out half its true size, so the angle is wrong.
30 is an area, not a side, so it cannot go into the cosine rule. The area formula uses it directly.

optionNotes.option: The cosine rule with the two sides
optionNotes.why: The cosine rule needs three sides, or two sides and the angle; here the angle is the unknown and the third side is missing. The area is the extra fact to use.

optionNotes.option: Nothing can be found until the third side is known
optionNotes.why: The given area is the missing piece: put the area formula equal to it and only sin C is unknown.

md: **Two triangles sharing a side** (Summer 2019, January 2020, Summer 2023). The answer's triangle has too little; its neighbour has enough. Find the shared side there first, then cross over.
**The area given, not asked** (November 2022, November 2023, Summer 2025). Put $\tfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ equal to the area and solve for the missing angle or side.
**Bearings** (Summer 2022, November 2025). Turn the bearings into an angle inside the triangle first: the back bearing, then a difference, or an angle at a north line.
**A quadrilateral** (Summer 2024, November 2024, November 2025). Draw a diagonal to make two triangles; the diagonal is the shared side.

stem: $X$ is $8.6$ km from $Y$ and $5.2$ km from $Z$. Seen from $Y$, $X$ lies on a bearing of $034°$, and angle $XZY = 31°$. Find the bearing of $Z$ from $Y$.

steps.decision: $XY = 8.6$ faces the $31°$ at $Z$: a complete pair. $XZ = 5.2$ faces $Y$.
Multiply by 5.2, then the inverse sine.
$Z$ lies clockwise of $X$ as seen from $Y$, so the angle adds to the bearing. Give it as three figures: $052°$.

prompt: The bearing of $Y$ from $X$ is $063°$; from $Y$ the next leg runs on a bearing of $145°$ to $Z$. What is angle $XYZ$, in degrees?
explain: Turn round at $Y$: the bearing of $X$ from $Y$ is $063° + 180° = 243°$. Both legs are now measured from the north line at $Y$, so angle $XYZ = 243° - 145° = 98°$. Subtracting the two given bearings, $82°$, measures nothing in the triangle.

twin.prompt: The bearing of $Q$ from $P$ is $115°$; from $Q$ the next leg runs on a bearing of $210°$ to $R$. What is angle $PQR$, in degrees?
twin.explain: The bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is $115° + 180° = 295°$. Both directions are measured from the north line at $Q$, so angle $PQR = 295° - 210° = 85°$.

md: The closing questions chain two or three rules, and the hardest part is the first step. Find the triangle with enough information, work out what it can give its neighbour (a side, usually, and sometimes an area), and carry that across. Keep every value at full calculator accuracy between the stages; round once, at the end.

title: Find the triangle that can start
md: When CCEA set a chain of trigonometry in Summer 2023, nearly 40% finished it, but over 40% could not find the first step at all. Look for the triangle with three known pieces before writing any rule.

stem: $PQRS$ has an area of $58$ cm$^2$. $SR = 10$ cm, $RQ = 8$ cm, angle $SRQ = 64°$ and $PS = 7$ cm. Calculate angle $PSQ$, correct to 1 decimal place.

steps.decision: Triangle $SQR$ has two sides and the angle between them: it can start.
The quadrilateral is the two triangles together.
The shared side, by the cosine rule, from the same triangle.
Keep the display: it is used again.
In $PSQ$ the area, $SQ$ and $PS$ are known: the area formula, backwards.
Inverse sine once, rounded at the end.

prompt: A length comes out as $7.483921\ldots$ cm and is needed in the next stage. What do you use?
options: The full value on the display
answer: The full value on the display
explain: As in steps 4 and 5 of See it: the length is carried at full accuracy into the next rule. Round only on the answer line; a rounded length fed forward moves the answer and costs the accuracy mark.

twin.prompt: A side comes out as $12.06475\ldots$ cm and is needed in the next stage. What do you use?
options: The unrounded value from the calculator's memory
twin.answer: The unrounded value from the calculator's memory
twin.explain: Store the value, or use the answer key, so the next stage gets every digit; round only on the answer line.

optionNotes.why: Two decimal places looks careful, but it is still a rounded value fed forward, and the final answer can move.
Rounding before the last stage changes the final answer, often in its last figure, and loses the accuracy mark.
Three significant figures is right for an answer line, not for a value that is used again. Keep the display.
Rounding this early moves every later result, and the final accuracy mark goes.

md: The formula sheet prints the cosine rule only in the form that finds a side. The form for an angle is two lines of rearranging away, and doing it yourself is safer than remembering a fraction: move the $2bc\cos A$ term so it is positive, then divide by everything multiplying $\cos A$.

stem: Rearrange $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$ to make $\cos A$ the subject.

steps.decision: Add $2bc\cos A$ to both sides, so the term is positive.
Subtract $a^2$ from both sides.
Divide both sides by $2bc$. The side facing $A$ is the one subtracted.

prompt: Rearrange $q^2 = p^2 + r^2 - 2pr\cos Q$ to make $\cos Q$ the subject.
explain: As in See it: add $2pr\cos Q$ and subtract $q^2$ on both sides, giving $2pr\cos Q = p^2 + r^2 - q^2$, then divide by $2pr$. The side facing $Q$, which is $q$, is the one subtracted.

twin.prompt: Rearrange $y^2 = x^2 + z^2 - 2xz\cos Y$ to make $\cos Y$ the subject.
twin.explain: Add $2xz\cos Y$ and subtract $y^2$: $2xz\cos Y = x^2 + z^2 - y^2$. Dividing by $2xz$ gives the result, with $y$, the side facing $Y$, subtracted.

optionNotes.why: All three signs on top are reversed. Make the cos Y term positive first, and the rest falls into place.
Only the 2 has been divided out. $\cos Y$ is multiplied by $2xz$, so divide by all of it.
Every sign on top has flipped. Making the $2pr\cos Q$ term positive first keeps $p^2 + r^2$ positive and $q^2$ subtracted.
Moving $q^2$ across the equals sign changes its sign, so it is subtracted, not added.

md:
Label any triangle so each side faces its angle.
Use the sine rule when a side faces a known angle, for a side or an angle.
Use the cosine rule for two sides and the angle between them, or three sides.
Find an area with ½ab sin C, or run it backwards from a given area.
Chain the rules across a shared side, from bearings or a quadrilateral.

Paper 2 only, usually twice: a single rule for three or four marks, then a chain of rules for six to eight near the end. The first mark is for the right rule written with its numbers in; the last is for the answer to the accuracy asked. Stuck: label the triangle, find the one with three known pieces, and start there.
